title: Krishna Urges Arjuna to Slay the Distressed Karna
story:
It was the war at Kurukshetra, and all through that long afternoon the sky had been turning into a net of arrows. Arjuna and Karna, the son of the charioteer Adhiratha, had been searching for each other's one lapse, and neither had yet given it. The two hosts had fallen back to watch, for it seemed the whole long war had narrowed at last to these two men alone, each of whom was desirous of availing himself of the other's lapses.

Arjuna had loosed a weapon that swelled with energy and went careering through the air with the effulgence of lightning, consuming the Kuru ranks, and the broken divisions of the Kauravas fled and stood at a distance, gazing at it. Karna alone held his ground. With showers of shafts winged with gold he baffled that burning weapon while it was still in the sky, and with a foe-killing weapon of his own, the great weapon he had obtained from Rama and which resembled in its efficacy an Atharvan rite, he crushed it and pierced Arjuna with keen shafts. Bending his own loud-sounding bow of unbreakable string, he shot showers of arrows, and the two of them closed.

They struck at each other like two fierce elephants striking with their tusks. The points of the compass became shrouded with weapons and the very sun went invisible. The sky turned into one vast arrowy net with no space between, and all the Kauravas and the Somakas beheld that wide-spread arrowy net, and in that dense darkness caused by arrows the two armies could make out nothing else. Those two foremost of men, both accomplished in weapons, kept aiming and shooting, and displayed diverse kinds of beautiful manoeuvres. Sometimes the Suta's son prevailed over his rival, sometimes the diadem-decked Arjuna prevailed, in prowess and weapons and lightness of hands, and every warrior on the field was filled with wonder. Even the beings in the welkin applauded, crying sometimes, Excellent, O Karna, and sometimes, Excellent, O Arjuna. And a serpent named Aswasena, who nursed an old hatred of Arjuna, had slipped into that arrowy darkness and was waiting there for his moment.

Then the turn came. The earth had been pressed deep all day with the weight of cars and the tread of steeds and elephants, and now it seemed to turn against one of its own. Karna's chariot wheel sank into the earth, and the ground held it, as though it had at last chosen its side. Karna stood stupefied. The man who had never shown his back in battle was held motionless in the open, in the sight of both hosts, and he could not draw his car free.

He called out to Arjuna and appealed to his righteousness. He was in distress, he said; he had been brought low not by his enemy's hand but by the ground itself. He did not ask for mercy, only for time, the chance to free his wheel and face Arjuna as an equal, as the dharma of warriors required. Let Arjuna remember dharma, he urged. Grant him one moment's respite, the bare moment that a warrior in his place could rightly claim.

Krishna, the younger brother of Indra, did not let the moment pass. Why, O son of Pandu, dost thou become so forgetful? he addressed him, with great excitement. They that are truly wise never spare their foes, however weak, even for a moment. Slay him, therefore, like Indra slaying the Asura Namuci.

Arjuna's arrow answered, and the warrior who had asked for a moment received none. The wheel stayed where the earth held it, and the duel was over.
reflection: The two pleas stand side by side and the account does not step in to say which was right. Karna asks for what dharma owes a man brought low; Krishna answers that a war is no place for such debts, and names Indra and Namuci as the precedent. That the episode ends without resolving the argument is, perhaps, the point: the hardest questions are the ones the source leaves open.
content_note: A warrior is slain in battle; the death is described with restraint.
next_story_tease: But the war's grief was not finished; a mother's curse was about to fall upon Krishna.
hero_scene: Karna standing motionless beside his chariot, its wheel sunk into the earth, calling out to Arjuna while Krishna urges Arjuna to strike, the sky above them dark with a net of arrows.
